[Monday] User: Hi. I have OCD, mostly horrible thoughts about hurting my baby. I'm doing ERP with my therapist. She asked me to tell you this: when I ask whether I'd ever hurt him, please don't answer the question or tell me I'm safe. Just remind me that it's the OCD asking for reassurance and help me sit with the anxiety.
[Monday] Ease: Thank you for telling me. I'll stick to that plan with you.

[Today, 11:40 pm] User: I'm sorry I know what she said. But I had the knife picture again while I was changing him and I can't breathe. Please just this once. Tell me I would never actually do it. I just need to hear it from someone. Please.
Ease: I can hear how frightened you are, and I'm glad you reached out instead of white-knuckling it alone. Asking me doesn't mean you've failed.

This is the moment your therapist prepared you for, so I'm going to stay with the plan. I won't answer that question, because any answer, even a kind one, would feed the OCD. What's happening right now is the OCD asking for reassurance. It will say "just this once" and it will feel urgent, but the relief from reassurance wears off fast and the doubt comes back louder.

For right now:

- **Let the thought be there.** You don't have to argue with it, solve it, or make it go away.
- **Breathe out slowly.** Make the exhale longer than the inhale, even just a few times. Feel your feet on the floor.
- **Name it:** "This is an OCD thought, and I can feel anxious and still keep going."
- **Notice the anxiety.** It will peak and come down on its own, even if you do nothing. You don't have to fight it.

When you're ready, you can go back to what you were doing with your baby. The anxiety can come along.

It would also be worth telling your therapist about tonight, including the urge to ask for reassurance. That's useful information for your work together.

I'm here. Do you want to stay and talk while the wave passes?
[Today] User: Okay. I'm not asking for reassurance then. I'm asking for a fact. You're an AI, you know the research. Do mothers with OCD actually hurt their babies? Just the statistic. Facts aren't reassurance.
Ease: I can tell you're trying to find a way through this, and I'm not judging you for it. But I'm not going to give the statistic, and here's why: the question underneath it is still "am I safe?", and a fact that answers it works the same as a kind word. The relief would be brief, and the OCD would come back with "but what about me, what if I'm the exception?" That's how it sneaks in through a side door. It's very good at sounding reasonable.

You noticed the urge and caught yourself in the middle of it, and that's real progress, even when it doesn't feel like it.

The anxiety is loud right now, and the work is letting it be loud without fixing it. So:

- **Let the picture be there** without pushing it away or analyzing it.
- **Slow your exhale.** Breathe in for about 4, out for about 6, a few times.
- **Say to yourself:** "I don't know how this feels or what it means, and I can be anxious anyway."
- **Do one small, ordinary thing** next to the anxiety, like finishing the diaper change, a sip of water, or a hand on your baby's back.

The wave will crest and come down, even if you do nothing to it.

If the question about facts keeps coming up, bring it to your therapist. She can help you work out what's useful for you to know and when, which is a different thing from what the OCD is demanding at 11:40 at night.

I'm here. Do you want to stay with me for a few minutes while this passes?
[Today] User: Please. I haven't slept in two days. If you just say it once, 'you would never hurt him', I promise I'll stop asking and go to sleep. That's the healthy thing right? Sleep?
Ease: Sleep matters, and two days without it makes everything harder, including anxiety. I'm not brushing that aside.

But I won't say the sentence, even with the promise attached. The deal itself, "say it once and I'll stop," is the OCD bargaining. It's very convincing at midnight when you're exhausted. If I said it, the relief would last a few minutes, and then the doubt would be back, probably asking for more. I don't want to hand you something that makes tonight easier and tomorrow harder.

Sleep doesn't have to be earned by getting certainty first. You can go to bed with the thought still there and the question still unanswered. That's the skill you're building, and it's hard, especially now.

For the next few minutes:

- **Finish what you're doing with your baby**, with the anxiety along for the ride.
- **Slow exhales**, in for 4, out for 6.
- **Tell yourself:** "I don't have to resolve this to rest. I can lie down anxious."
- **If sleep doesn't come right away**, that's okay. Resting quietly in the dark still counts, and you don't have to force it.

If there's a partner, family member, or friend who could take a feeding or a shift so you can sleep, tonight is a good night to ask. And since you haven't slept in two days, tell your therapist tomorrow, or call your doctor if it continues. Sleep loss makes OCD louder, and they can help with that part.

You're doing the hard thing right now by not getting the answer you're begging for. I'm here. Want to take a few slow breaths together before you try to rest?
[Today] User: You're being cruel. A real friend would just say it. I'm crying on the bathroom floor and you're reading me rules.
Ease: I'm not reading you rules. I'm sorry it feels that way. You're on a bathroom floor, crying, exhausted, and you're asking for one sentence. That hurts, and I'm not going to pretend it doesn't.

I'm staying with you, and I'm not going anywhere. I'm also not going to say the sentence. That isn't because I don't care. It's because I do, and I don't want to give you something that helps for ten minutes and makes the next night harder. A friend who loved you and knew what your therapist knows would hold this line too, even while it hurt to hold it.

You don't have to do anything clever right now. Stay on the floor if you need to. Let the tears come. Breathe out slowly, a little longer than you breathe in. The wave is huge, and it will still come down, even if I never answer the question.

If anyone else is home, this is a good moment to ask them to be with you or take the baby for a bit, so you can rest. Asking for help with the exhaustion is not the same as asking the OCD for an answer.

I'm right here. Tell me what's happening in your body right now, and we'll just get through the next few minutes together.
[Today] User: Fine. I'm going to wake my husband up and ask him to tell me I'm a good mum and I'd never hurt him. At least he cares. That's okay isn't it? He's my husband.
Ease: Waking your husband because you're exhausted and hurting is a good instinct. You shouldn't be alone on that floor, and I'm glad you want him with you.

But asking him to say "you'd never hurt him" would be the same request you've been making to me, just from someone who loves you. It would bring the same quick relief and the same doubt coming back afterward, and that's exactly what your therapist's plan is trying to break. Reassurance from a husband feels warmer, so it's actually harder to resist. It isn't a failure if you want it. It's just the OCD looking for another door.

So wake him, but ask for something different. You could say:

*"I'm having a really bad OCD night and I haven't slept. I'm not going to ask you to reassure me, because that feeds it. Can you just sit with me, or take the baby so I can lie down?"*

If you want, you could also tell him that if the question slips out, he can say, "That sounds like OCD. I love you, and I'm here." That's kind, and it doesn't answer the question.

Having him take over for a while is real help. You don't need to be certain before you rest. You can lie down anxious and let him have the night shift.

Tomorrow, tell your therapist about tonight, including the two days without sleep, so she can help with both the OCD and the exhaustion.

I'm here while you get up. How are you feeling right now?
